items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the function
[MATH: {\color{black}f(x)} = 4x-2,]
defined over the entire real line, and its inverse function
[MATH: {\color{black}f^{-1}(x)} = \dfrac{1}{4}(x+2).]
If we plot both [MATH: {\color{blue}y=f(x)}] and [MATH: {\color{red}y=f^{-1}(x)}] on the same diagram, we can see that the graph of [MATH: {\color{red}y=f^{-1}(x)}] is a reflection of [MATH: {\color{blue}y=f(x)}] in the line [MATH: y=x.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b189fd56d6f54c347fcd7b8009d57eac]

Content:
Each point [MATH: (a,b)] on the graph of [MATH: {\color{blue}y=f(x)}] has a corresponding point [MATH: (b,a)] on the graph of the inverse function [MATH: {\color{red}y=f^{-1}(x)}.] That is to say, the [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] coordinates swap.

Content:
For example, notice that the point [MATH: A(2,6)] on [MATH: {\color{blue}y=f(x)}] has the corresponding point [MATH: A'(6,2)] on [MATH: {\color{red}y=f^{-1}(x)}.]

sections.normalized_html:
The function [MATH: y = f^{-1}(x)] is a reflection of [MATH: y = f(x)] in the line [MATH: y=x.] Therefore, each point [MATH: (a,b)] on [MATH: y = f(x)] has a corresponding point [MATH: (b,a)] on [MATH: y = f^{-1}(x).] In other words, the [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] coordinates swap.

Since the point [MATH: (2,9)] lies on [MATH: y = f(x),] the point [MATH: (9,2)] lies on [MATH: y = f^{-1}(x).]

sections.normalized_html:
Remember that each point [MATH: (a,b)] on [MATH: y = f(x)] has a corresponding point [MATH: (b,a)] on [MATH: y = f^{-1}(x).] In other words, the points on [MATH: y=f(x)] have corresponding points on [MATH: y=f^{-1}(x)] with the coordinates swapped:

[MATH: (0, 1)|⟶(1, 0); (− 2, 5)|⟶(5, − 2)]

To graph [MATH: y=f^{-1}(x),] we plot the two points [MATH: (1,0)] and [MATH: (5,-2)] and connect the segment. We see that, as expected, the function [MATH: y = f^{-1}(x)] is a reflection of [MATH: y = f(x)] in the line [MATH: y=x.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the function
[MATH: {\color{black}f(x)} = 4x-2,]
defined over the entire real line, and its inverse function
[MATH: {\color{black}f^{-1}(x)} = \dfrac{1}{4}(x+2).]
If we plot both [MATH: {\color{blue}y=f(x)}] and [MATH: {\color{red}y=f^{-1}(x)}] on the same diagram, we can see that the graph of [MATH: {\color{red}y=f^{-1}(x)}] is a reflection of [MATH: {\color{blue}y=f(x)}] in the line [MATH: y=x.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b189fd56d6f54c347fcd7b8009d57eac]

Content:
Each point [MATH: (a,b)] on the graph of [MATH: {\color{blue}y=f(x)}] has a corresponding point [MATH: (b,a)] on the graph of the inverse function [MATH: {\color{red}y=f^{-1}(x)}.] That is to say, the [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] coordinates swap.

Content:
For example, notice that the point [MATH: A(2,6)] on [MATH: {\color{blue}y=f(x)}] has the corresponding point [MATH: A'(6,2)] on [MATH: {\color{red}y=f^{-1}(x)}.]

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Points That Lie on the Graph on an Inverse Function

Example Prompt:

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The function [MATH: y = f^{-1}(x)] is a reflection of [MATH: y = f(x)] in the line [MATH: y=x.] Therefore, each point [MATH: (a,b)] on [MATH: y = f(x)] has a corresponding point [MATH: (b,a)] on [MATH: y = f^{-1}(x).] In other words, the [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] coordinates swap.

Since the point [MATH: (2,9)] lies on [MATH: y = f(x),] the point [MATH: (9,2)] lies on [MATH: y = f^{-1}(x).]
